segments: ️ The pain of the traditional approach

On Arch Linux, if you install gcc, libxml2, libxslt to compile a Python project, those packages remain in the global environment until explicitly removed, and may cause version conflicts between projects. On NixOS: You can define an environment in the project directory and return to the outer shell when you exit; objects in the store remain until garbage collection removes them.
In a modern workflow, we define the environment in the project’s flake.nix:
Manually running nix develop every time is tedious. With direnv, the environment loads automatically as soon as you enter the directory.
Create an .envrc in the project root:
Run direnv allow once. The next time you cd into this directory, the terminal will automatically display direnv: loading..., and all your tools and environment variables will be ready!
Version isolation: Project A uses Python 3.9 and project B uses Python 3.12, without interfering with each other.

Team consistency: Share flake.nix, flake.lock, and .envrc with your colleagues, and match the target platform. The lock file pins input revisions, while running services, external downloads, and system state can still affect the actual result.

direnv allow authorizes the .envrc in the current directory to execute shell code, so read it first. Home Manager configuration must be paired with the appropriate shell integration. Changing directories restores environment variables; it does not automatically stop a database started by shellHook.
